english.html: enemy <sup class="mk" data-key="k">k</sup>. Nay, even though the enmity should not appear, if he is ever so little suspected of it <sup class="mk" data-key="l">l</sup>. And the reason may easily be gathered from what Cicero has eloquently left in writing. Our ancestors, he says, did not wish to open this road to enmities, that it should be lawful for anyone to injure his enemy by his testimony; inasmuch as men are so far carried by passion in the hatred they bear to another, that they would readily advance and fabricate a thousand lies to injure him <sup class="mk" data-key="m">m</sup>. In which Cicero shows that he had in no wise caught the scent of the Christian Law, by which it is commanded — not, as the Scribes and Pharisees thought and taught it to be written in the old law: Thou shalt love thy neighbour, and hate thine enemy <sup class="mk" data-key="n">n</sup> — but more holily, to love our enemies, bless them that curse us, do good to them that hate us, pray for them that calumniate and persecute us, that we may be children of our Father which is in heaven <sup class="mk" data-key="o">o</sup>,

notes.citation: Digest 22.5.3 pr. (De testibus, l. 3 at the beginning); Decretals, X 5.1 (De accusationibus), cc. Repellatur, Qualiter (presumably Qualiter et quando) and Cum oporteat — chapter numbers unverified

notes.gloss: D. 22.5.3 (Callistratus): the judge is to weigh each witness's standing, "whether he is an enemy of the man against whom he testifies".

notes.citation: Decretals, title De accusationibus (X 5.1), c. Cum, at the § Maconella — unidentified: no chapter Cum with a paragraph of that name was found; Mãconella may be a wrong sort
notes.original: c. cũ. P. Mãconella de accuſatio.
Ciceron en l'oraiſon pro-Fotcio & aux partitions.
notes.gloss: The Pro Fonteio is Cicero's attack on the hostile Gallic witnesses; the sentence Coras paraphrases, that "our ancestors" would not let an enemy's testimony hurt a man, was not located in either work and may be a free rendering; the rule itself is that of the Lex Iulia at D. 22.5.3.5 and of the title De accusationibus cited at {k}.
Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself; the "and hate thine enemy" is the Pharisees' addition reported at Matthew 5:43, as Coras says.

notes.original: S. Math. c. v. S. Luc vi.
notes.gloss: Love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you, pray for them that despitefully use you and persecute you, that ye may be the children of your Father which is in heaven.

english.html: Making a particular enumeration of the whole, together with what was owed to him, and by what persons.

From this may arise a fine and noble question: whether credit ought to be given to the assertion of the said du Tilh, made at the hour of his end, and whether sufficient proof may be gathered from it of what he confessed to owe, or affirmed to be owed to him. On which the most certain and common resolution is that the assertion, saying or declaration of one who is about to die, although it makes proof to his own prejudice, or to that of his heir <sup class="mk" data-key="a">a</sup>, is nevertheless invalid and of no effect whatever to the disadvantage of another <sup class="mk" data-key="b">b</sup>. And indeed, as it is reasonable that each should be believed in what he attests against himself <sup class="mk" data-key="c">c</sup>, so it would be beyond reason that credit should be given him to the prejudice of another <sup class="mk" data-key="d">d</sup>; yes, even though it were the father or the mother who, in their last days, attested something against their own

notes.citation: Digest 32 (De legatis et fideicommissis [III]; Coras's de lega. iij.), l. Cum quis decedens § Codicillis; Digest 39.5 (De donationibus), l. Ex hac scriptura
notes.original: l. cũ quis de cedens. P. codicillis. D. de lega. iij. l. ex hac ſcriptura. D. de donatio.
notes.gloss: Fragment numbers not verified. Both cited for a dying man's written acknowledgment binding his own heir.

notes.original: l. ſæpe. D. de re iudi.
notes.gloss: Saepe constitutum est res inter alios iudicatas aliis non praeiudicare: what is decided between some does not prejudice others.

notes.citation: Digest 11.1 (De interrogationibus in iure faciendis), l. De aetate § 1 (cf. D. 11.1.11); Digest 16.3 (Depositi vel contra; Coras's de poſ.), l. Publia (D. 16.3.26, Paulus, Publia Maevia), last §
notes.original: l. de ætate P i. D. de interrog. actio. l. Publia. P. dernier. D. de poſ.
notes.gloss: A party's answer under interrogation, and a written acknowledgment, bind the one who made them.

notes.citation: Digest 16.1 (Ad senatus consultum Velleianum), l. Seia; Code 4.19 (De probationibus), l. Rationes
notes.original: l. Seia D. ad Velleia l. rationes C. de prob.
notes.gloss: Fragment numbers not verified. A debtor's own accounts or acknowledgment do not prove against a third party.
